title: Surasa's open mouth
hookLine: the gods decide to test Hanuman, and send the mother of serpents with her mouth wide open; why Hindus pray to him for wisdom too
carry: bal and buddhi: strength and wisdom together

cards: A coach who keeps raising the bar every time you clear it. Some tests aren't trying to stop you; they're trying to see what you do when force won't work.
Over the open sea, Mainaka behind him, Hanuman flies straight into one of those. And the ones who set it up aren't his enemies. They're the gods, who want to know what this monkey is really made of.

teach.h: THE GODS ASK SURASA TO TEST HIM.
teach.b: The gods, the celestial musicians and the great sages talk it over.
They ask Surasa, the mother of the nagas, the serpent beings, to take a terrifying form and block Hanuman's way, so they can see his strength and his cleverness.
Surasa rises from the sea: the gods have given you to me as food, she says. You have to enter my mouth.
Hanuman doesn't attack. He talks. He tells her who he is and why he's here: Rama, Sita taken, the search.
Then he makes a remarkable offer. Let me find Sita and tell Rama, and I promise I'll come back and enter your mouth. Surasa refuses.
She has a boon, she says, that no one can get past her. And she opens her mouth.
So Hanuman grows to ten yojanas, too big to swallow. She opens wider, twenty. He grows to thirty; she opens to forty.
On they go, until her mouth gapes a hundred yojanas wide. Every time he gets bigger, she gets bigger. Remember why the gods sent her: to see his strength and his buddhi, his intelligence.
That pairing is why Hanuman is prayed to the way he is.
Near its opening, the Hanuman Chalisa asks him: bal buddhi bidya dehu mohi.
Give me strength, wisdom and learning. Hindu students say that line before exams, and grandparents say it over them. Strength alone has only made Surasa's mouth bigger.
Hanuman, hovering there, has to think of something else.

how: Storytellers telling the Sundara Kanda often pause on Surasa's growing mouth before revealing how Hanuman gets through, and many Hindu students say the Chalisa's 'bal buddhi bidya' line before exams.

o: a river goddess who carries him to the shore
a sea demon who catches him by his shadow
the serpent mother the gods send to test Hanuman

p: let me finish, then I'll come back
strength, wisdom, learning: the Chalisa's ask

s: Surasa is sent by Ravana to stop Hanuman
the gods and sages ask her to test his strength and wit.
the Hanuman Chalisa asks him for strength only
it asks for bal, buddhi and bidya: strength, wisdom and learning.
every time he grows, Surasa opens her mouth wider.

games.q: the night before a big test, Nani says the Chalisa line 'bal buddhi bidya dehu mohi' over you. why ask the strong god for this?
o: Hanuman is strength and wisdom together; the gods even tested his buddhi with Surasa.
because exams are a kind of fight you win by force.
it's just habit; any line would do.
games.why: the gods sent Surasa to see his strength and his buddhi. the Chalisa asks him for both, plus learning.

practice: If you know it, say quietly the line many students say before an exam: bal buddhi bidya dehu mohi. Strength, wisdom, learning. Breathe in on bal, hold on buddhi, breathe out on bidya.
If you'd rather not pray, bring to mind one problem where pushing harder keeps making it worse, let the breath get smaller and slower, and ask what wisdom would do instead.

wordCard.voice: Surasa. The mother of serpents, sent by the gods to test Hanuman, whose mouth grows wider every time he grows bigger, until force can't win.

orig.note: Sanskrit surasā, the name of the mother of the nāgas in this story.

carryVoice: Your line: bal and buddhi, strength and wisdom together. His answer comes tomorrow. Day six hundred eight, done.
